## Revelation 1 – Research Notes

**v. 1**
- Guzik: "Revelation" (*apokalupsis*) means an unveiling. The book is Jesus' revelation in two senses: He gives it, and He is what it reveals. Its signs make sense against the Old Testament, which it alludes to more than 500 times. The best evidence points to the Apostle John as the author. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-1/
- Ellicott: John is the writer but Christ is the author. Christ acts all through the book, for example opening the seals. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/revelation-1.html
- **Where readers differ on "soon / shortly":**
  - Guzik lists the four main approaches (preterist, historicist, poetic, futurist). He grants each some truth but argues the futurist view can't be set aside. He also cites Walvoord: the phrase means things will happen suddenly once they begin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-1/
  - Ellicott admits the word gives preterists a "plausible" basis. He holds that the prophecy is fulfilled again and again through history, not used up in one era. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/revelation-1.html
  - Garland (Precept Austin) weighs three options. He rejects the preterist one, which says everything happened in the first readers' lifetimes. He prefers "imminent from God's point of view" to "swift once begun." https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-1-commentary
  - Garland also asks whether the revelation is *from* Christ or *about* Christ. He thinks the context points to "from." https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-1-commentary

**v. 2**
- Guzik: by calling his book "the word of God," John shows he knew he was writing Scripture. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-1/
- Ellicott: "witness" and "testimony" are favourite words in John's Gospel and letters, which links this book to them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/revelation-1.html

**v. 3**
- Guzik: this is the first of seven blessings in Revelation. One person reads and many listen, which reflects the church's public reading of Scripture. Readers are blessed even without understanding everything. He adds that the Anglican Church largely leaves Revelation out of its regular readings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-1/
- Ellicott: the call to "keep" what is written suggests the book applies in every age, neither all in the past nor all in the future. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/revelation-1.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik: the greeting comes from all three Persons of the Trinity. "Who is and was and is to come" echoes the name Yahweh. The "seven Spirits" are the Holy Spirit in fullness, drawing on the seven-fold description of the Spirit in Isaiah 11:2. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-1/
- Ellicott:
  - The odd grammar is deliberate, a way of rendering the divine name.
  - He rejects the view that the seven Spirits are seven chief angels.
  - He also rejects the view of Vitringa and others that the seven churches stand for seven ages of church history. Instead, quoting Chrysostom and Augustine, the seven stand for the whole church.
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/revelation-1.html
- GotQuestions says Scripture doesn't spell out who the seven spirits are. My excerpt stopped before its conclusion. https://www.gotquestions.org/seven-spirits-God.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik:
  - The Greek word for "witness" is also the word for martyr.
  - "Firstborn" means first in rank, not created.
  - The past-tense reading "loved us" points back to the cross.
  - Manuscripts differ between "washed" and "loosed," and both are true.
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-1/
- Ellicott: Christ is the present ruler of kings, not only the future one. He prefers the reading "washed." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/revelation-1.html

**v. 6**
- Guzik: believers are royalty and also priests with access to God. In the Old Testament the offices of king and priest were kept apart, but believers now share both, as Christ does. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-1/
- Ellicott: the washing language leads into priestly consecration. The book's songs of praise grow from two parts here to seven by chapter 7. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/revelation-1.html

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: the verse echoes Mark 14:62 and Zechariah 12:10. He notes that Augustine read the "clouds" as a picture of the saints. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/revelation-1.html
- Coffman: the link to Zechariah is only in the wording. Here people grieve for themselves, not for the one who was pierced. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/1-7.html
- BibleHub Q&A: the verse describes a literal, worldwide future event, not a symbol of spiritual experience. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_every_eye_will_see_Him.htm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: the words "the beginning and the ending" were probably copied in later from 22:13. The verse refers to Christ and strongly affirms His deity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/revelation-1.html

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: John was probably an exile free to move about Patmos, sent there for preaching. His message set the God-man against the Roman worship of the emperor as a man-god. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/revelation-1.html

**v. 10**
- **Most sources read "the Lord's day" as Sunday:**
  - GotQuestions. https://www.gotquestions.org/Lords-day.html
  - Clarke calls it the Christian Sabbath. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/1-10.html
  - The BibleHub Q&A cites Ignatius and Justin Martyr. https://biblehub.com/q/What_is_the_Lord_s_Day_in_Rev_1_10.htm
- **Views these sources argue against:**
  - Ellicott rejects the futurist reading that the phrase means "the Day of the Lord." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/revelation-1.html
  - Coffman rejects both the judgment-day and the Saturday-Sabbath readings. He quotes Dake that the term may have been a protest against Caesar-worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/1-10.html
  - Guzik suggests the same idea, linking it to the Roman "Emperor's Day." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-1/
- **"In the Spirit":**
  - Guzik (Pentecostal-leaning site): a unique experience of revelation from the Holy Spirit, which happens four times in the book. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-1/
  - 1517 (Lutheran) is more ordinary: John was reading, hearing and keeping the Word in Sunday worship, as any Christian might. https://www.1517.org/articles/revelation-110a-in-the-spirit-008

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: there were more than seven churches, so seven stands for completeness. The list follows the route a messenger would take from Patmos. The added words "I am Alpha and Omega" are missing from the best manuscripts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/revelation-1.html

**vv. 12–16** (Ellicott only) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/revelation-1.html
- **v. 12:** The lampstands probably looked like the familiar seven-branched lampstand, suggesting separate churches united in Christ.
- **v. 13:** The long robe is a high priest's robe, and the gold sash shows royalty at rest. Together they show Christ as King-Priest.
- **v. 14:** The white hair stands for wisdom and age, as with the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7. The fiery eyes mean He is set on burning away evil.
- **v. 15:** The bronze is metal at white heat. The voice like many waters is the voice that once stilled the sea.
- **v. 16:** The stars in His hand show how precious the churches are to Him and how He cares for them. The sword is His word, the only weapon His kingdom needs.

**v. 20 – Who are the "angels"?**
- **Pastors or ministers:** Barnes concludes they are the pastor or presiding elder, not a bishop over several churches. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/1-20.html
- **Guardian angels:** the BibleHub commentary page argues against this, since the letters scold and encourage them. That page also calls the stars "emblems of the ministers," but the excerpt didn't show who wrote that. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/1-20.htm
- **Heavenly beings:** the BibleHub Q&A describes this view. https://biblehub.com/q/who_are_the_seven_church_angels.htm
- **Human messengers or guardian angels:** GotQuestions weighs both. My excerpt cut off before its preferred answer. https://www.gotquestions.org/seven-stars-Revelation.html

To fill the gaps, the next sources to read would be Gill and the Pulpit Commentary for vv. 7–20 (on biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/1-x.htm), the NET Bible notes, and newadvent.org and oca.org.
